knowledge_point.title: Expressions Containing a Negative Linear Term

question.:question/worked-solution:
The half of the linear coefficient is $-\frac{3}{2}$. **Add and subtract** its square so the expression keeps its value.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^2-3x+2&=\underbrace{x^2-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+\frac{9}{4}}_{\text{perfect square}}-\frac{9}{4}+2 \\
&=\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2-\frac{9}{4}+2 \\
&=\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2-\frac{1}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The minus sign inside the square produces the required linear term $-3x$.

The blanks are $\frac{3}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$; the sign before the second blank is already supplied.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Put the quadratic term first: $2-3x+x^2=x^2-3x+2$.

The half of the linear coefficient is $-\frac{3}{2}$. **Add and subtract** its square so the expression keeps its value.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^2-3x+2&=\underbrace{x^2-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+\frac{9}{4}}_{\text{perfect square}}-\frac{9}{4}+2 \\
&=\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2-\frac{9}{4}+2 \\
&=\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2-\frac{1}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The minus sign inside the square produces the required linear term $-3x$.

Comparing with $(x+a)^2+b$ gives $a=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $b=-\frac{1}{4}$.
